claim.text: Across extensive experiments on CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and CIFAR-10 using standard architectures and a broad set of unstructured sparsification methods, sparse neural networks trained on challenging samples often achieve test accuracy that matches or surpasses the corresponding dense models at particular overall sparsity ratios in the 10%–90% range.
The behavior described in claim 1 is observed for clean test accuracy.
The behavior described in claim 1 is observed, in adversarial training regimes, for adversarial accuracy (accuracy on perturbed test data) as well.

When training data are scarce (where the data ratio, the fraction of the challenging subset used for training, is reduced from the full set), sparse neural networks tend to outperform dense counterparts more markedly than in the full-data regime.
When training data are scarce, the advantage of sparse neural networks over dense counterparts is most pronounced at higher overall sparsity levels in the reported experiments.

Under adversarial training with Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), sparse models at high sparsity achieve comparable clean test accuracy compared to dense models on the examined benchmarks (VGG16 on CIFAR-10 and ResNet18 on CIFAR-100).

Under adversarial training with Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), sparse models at high sparsity achieve superior adversarial test accuracy compared to dense models on the examined benchmarks (VGG16 on CIFAR-10 and ResNet18 on CIFAR-100).
This trend, described in claim 6, claim 7, holds at both full and reduced data volumes tested in the paper.

Sparse methods that allocate higher relative density (proportion of non-zero weights) to early (shallower) layers tend to yield higher test accuracy on hard-sample training than uniform per-layer pruning.

Empirically, layer-wise density profiles (proportion of non-zero weights) with richer shallow-layer connectivity correlate with improved performance across training on EL2N-selected samples, corrupted images with common corruptions, and adversarial training scenarios (using PGD).
Methods that derive sparse topologies from pre-trained dense models can tolerate sparser shallow layers
pre-trained weights have already encoded low-level features
In the studied setup (one-shot pruning at initialization with rewinding to t=0), LTH sometimes exhibits degraded performance when trained on hard samples
masks produced from dense pre-training are not universally optimal for hard-sample regimes
whether a sparse method starts from a pre-trained dense model or from scratch materially affects performance on hard samples and interacts with the layer-wise density allocation

Dynamic-sparse training methods that form sparse topologies before or early during training achieve the dual benefit of test accuracy improvement and reduced training floating-point operations and parameter counts in the evaluated hard-sample regimes (EL2N-selected, corrupted, adversarial).
Dense-to-sparse procedures that require obtaining a fully trained dense model incur additional training floating-point operations (FLOPs) due to dense pre-training.
The sparse models resulting from dense-to-sparse procedures that require obtaining a fully trained dense model may have fewer parameters.

When training on inputs corrupted by common visible degradations, using 30% of the corrupted subset (a training data ratio of 0.3), the relative benefit of sparse neural networks (SNNs) over dense models grows as corruption severity increases from low to moderate levels (severity 2 to severity 4 on the 1–6 scale).
At extreme corruption severity (severity 6), the relative improvement of sparse neural networks (SNNs) over dense models shrinks or disappears for some sparse methods.

Across extensive experiments on CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and CIFAR-10 using standard architectures and a broad set of unstructured sparsification methods, sparse neural networks trained on intrinsically difficult examples selected by Error L2 Norm (EL2N) scores, images with common corruptions such as Gaussian noise and blurring, or adversarially perturbed inputs via Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) often achieve test accuracy that matches or surpasses the corresponding dense models at particular overall sparsity ratios in the 10%–90% range.

When training data are scarce (where the data ratio, the fraction of the challenging subset used for training, is reduced from the full set), both Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) using the Erdős–Rényi–Kernel (ERK) distribution and Single-shot Network Pruning (SNIP) using connection sensitivity pruning before training tend to outperform dense counterparts more markedly than in the full-data regime.
When training data are scarce, the advantage of sparse neural networks over dense counterparts is most pronounced at 70%–90% sparsity in the reported experiments.

Under adversarial training with Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), sparse models at 90% overall sparsity achieve comparable clean test accuracy compared to dense models on the examined benchmarks (VGG16 on CIFAR-10 and ResNet18 on CIFAR-100).
This trend, described in claim 6, claim 7, holds at both full data volumes and the data ratio of 0.5 tested in the paper.

Erdős–Rényi–Kernel (ERK) allocations used with Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) and the density patterns observed for Single-shot Network Pruning (SNIP), both of which allocate higher relative density (proportion of non-zero weights) to early (shallower) layers, tend to yield higher test accuracy on hard-sample training than uniform per-layer pruning.
One-shot Magnitude Pruning (OMP) after full dense training, and the one-shot variant of Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) using pruning at initialization can tolerate sparser shallow layers
In the studied setup (one-shot pruning at initialization with rewinding to t=0), LTH sometimes exhibits degraded performance when trained on EL2N-selected or corrupted samples
whether a sparse method starts from a pre-trained dense model or from scratch materially affects performance on EL2N-selected or corrupted samples and interacts with the layer-wise density allocation

The two dynamic-sparse training methods Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) with Erdős–Rényi–Kernel (ERK) distribution and Single-shot Network Pruning (SNIP), which form sparse topologies before or early during training, achieve the dual benefit of test accuracy improvement and reduced training floating-point operations and parameter counts in the evaluated hard-sample regimes (EL2N-selected, corrupted, adversarial).

The two dense-to-sparse procedures Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) with one-shot pruning at initialization and One-shot Magnitude Pruning (OMP) after full training, which require obtaining a fully trained dense model, incur additional training floating-point operations (FLOPs) due to dense pre-training.

When training on inputs corrupted by Gaussian noise, blurring, and impulse noise, using 30% of the corrupted subset (a training data ratio of 0.3), the relative benefit of sparse neural networks (SNNs) over dense models grows as corruption severity increases from low to moderate levels (severity 2 to severity 4 on the 1–6 scale).
